title: Integrated management of acute pulmonary embolism and the post-pulmonary embolism syndrome: risk stratification, modern therapies, and long-term follow-up.
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is increasingly recognized as an episode of care that extends well beyond hospital discharge. Current guidance is distributed across several documents: the 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines; the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline, which replaced the massive/submassive terminology with clinical categories A-E; and separate position papers on catheter-directed intervention (CDI) and on follow-up. This narrative review (i) provides a side-by-side comparison of the ESC and AHA/ACC risk frameworks and their therapeutic implications; (ii) updates the evidence on reperfusion, including the recent randomized trials HI-PEITHO, PEERLESS and STORM-PE; and (iii) focuses on transitions of care and long-term follow-up, which guidelines address less comprehensively. Anticoagulation, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant, remains the treatment for most patients. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (ESC) or category E (AHA/ACC) PE, because in intermediate-risk disease it halves hemodynamic decompensation at the cost of a several-fold increase in major and intracranial bleeding, without long-term functional benefit. In HI-PEITHO, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced a 7-day composite outcome driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (4.0% vs. 10.3%) in intermediate-high-risk patients with additional markers of physiological stress, without intracranial hemorrhage; a survival benefit of CDI has not been demonstrated. At discharge, a minimum bundle should specify the drug, dose, anticipated duration, provoking context, bleeding mitigation and follow-up ownership, followed by early contact within one week and a structured review at approximately three months. Up to half of survivors report persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation, whereas chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in approximately 2%-3%. Persistent symptoms should prompt phenotype-directed evaluation with echocardiography, ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and, when indicated, right-heart catheterization interpreted with the 2022 hemodynamic definitions, followed by early referral to an expert center where pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy can be combined. We state the type of evidence underpinning each key recommendation, propose a discharge bundle, a structured follow-up algorithm and episode-wide quality indicators, and identify the evidence gaps that should guide future trials.

title: Serial cardiac ultrasound in acutely ill adults: a systematic review.
abstract: Cardiopulmonary symptoms frequently prompt emergency department (ED) visits. Serial as-sessment of dynamic cardiac ultrasound parameters may support monitoring, but their asso-ciation with patient outcomes and role in guiding management is uncertain. This systematic review evaluated whether serial changes in ejection fraction (EF), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and the right ventricular-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) ratio are associated with mortality, readmissions, length of stay, or intensive care unit trans-fer in acutely ill patients. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase (Ovid), CENTRAL (Wiley), Scopus (Elsevier), Web of Science (Clarivate), Google Scholar, ProQuest, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the International Clini-cal Trials Registry Platform. The initial search was conducted on 16 April 2024 and updated on 31 October 2025. We included randomized and non-randomized trials and observational stud-ies of adults (≥18 years) undergoing at least two in-hospital cardiac ultrasound assessments and reported mortality, readmission, length of stay, and/or intensive care unit transfer. Risk of bias was assessed with study design-specific tools. Results were summarized using synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM). Of 15,174 screened records, 11 studies with a total of 941 patients were included. Study popu-lations were defined by presenting symptoms (dyspnea, hypotension) or by clinical conditions (toxicological, infectious, and cardiopulmonary diseases). Echocardiography was most used, and patients underwent 3-4 scans during admission. Overall risk of bias was moderate to high. Four studies compared serial changes in EF, TAPSE, and/or the RV/LV ratio with outcomes and found no consistent pattern. One randomized study evaluated ultrasound-guided treatment and found no difference compared with usual care. Across studies, EF, TAPSE, and RV/LV ratio were generally stable or improved over time. Available evidence is limited and does not demonstrate a consistent association between serial cardiac ultrasound parameters and outcomes in acutely ill adults. However, serial changes are frequently observed, highlighting the need for trials evaluating whether decision-linked, ultrasound-guided management strategies can improve outcomes. PROSPERO, CRD42024524740.

title: Utility of Point-of-care Ultrasound in Clinical Care: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has emerged as an essential bedside diagnostic tool in modern clinical practice. By enabling real-time visualization of anatomical structures and physiological processes, POCUS allows clinicians to rapidly evaluate patients and integrate imaging findings directly into clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the clinical utility of POCUS across both critical and noncritical care settings. Key applications include the use of structured ultrasound protocols during cardiac arrest, such as the US-CAB framework, and lung ultrasound approaches like the bedside lung ultrasound in emergency protocol for evaluating acute respiratory failure. In addition, growing evidence supports the use of POCUS in common emergency department presentations, including acute flank pain, nontraumatic abdominal pain, and undifferentiated chest pain or dyspnea. Across these clinical scenarios, POCUS has been shown to facilitate rapid diagnosis, reduce reliance on radiation-based imaging, and improve operational efficiency by shortening emergency department length of stay and expediting clinical decision-making. Despite its clinical advantages, the effective implementation of POCUS requires appropriate operator training and standardized protocols to ensure diagnostic reliability. Ongoing advances in portable ultrasound technology and image-analysis tools may further enhance the accessibility and clinical integration of POCUS in diverse healthcare environments. Overall, POCUS represents a valuable extension of bedside clinical assessment and continues to play an expanding role in modern patient-centered care.

title: [Tsutsugamushi disease with left heart failure as the main manifestation complicated by multiple organ dysfunction: a case report and literature review].
journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
abstract: Tsutsugamushi disease (TD) is a zoonotic and naturally focal infectious disease caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi (Ot), transmitted between humans and rodents through the bite of chigger mites. On August 17, 2025, a patient with TD complicated by acute left sided heart failure and multiple organ dysfunction was admitted to Wuhan Jinyintan Hospital. The patient presented to the emergency department with a 10 day history of fever, palpitations, dyspnea, and cough, and had a history of outdoor exposure. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 39.2 centigrade, a heart rate of 79 beats/min (showing relative bradycardia), an eschar of 0.5 cm×0.6 cm at the intersection of the right mid axillary line and the umbilical horizontal line, and a truncal rash. Laboratory findings showed an eosinophil count of 0, troponin T 1.31 μg/L, N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide 2 912.60 ng/L, and elevated procalcitonin. Electrocardiography revealed prolonged Q T and Q Tc intervals, and chest CT demonstrated bilateral interstitial pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusion. Next generation sequencing of blood detected Ot nucleic acid fragments, and serum Ot immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody was positive, confirming the diagnosis of TD complicated by myocarditis, acute left sided heart failure, and multiple organ dysfunction. The patient was treated with doxycycline combined with rifampicin for anti infection, along with symptomatic and supportive care, as well as local interventions including thoracentesis drainage and bronchoalveolar lavage. Subsequently, the patient's body temperature normalized, cardiac function improved, pulmonary edema and pleural effusion resolved, and myocardial enzymes returned to normal levels; the patient was discharged with clinical cure. This case indicates that TD can affect the cardiovascular system, presenting as acute left sided heart failure and myocarditis. For patients with fever, relative bradycardia, and multiple organ dysfunction, TD should be considered in the differential diagnosis, and early recognition of the eschar together with prompt initiation of etiological therapy are crucial for improving prognosis.

title: High-flow nasal cannula versus noninvasive ventilation in acute heart failure-related respiratory failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is the recommended first-line respiratory support for acute heart failure (AHF)-related respiratory failure. However, its tolerance is often limited. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) has emerged as a potential alternative, but comparative evidence remains inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HFNC versus NIV in patients with AHF-related respiratory failure. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA guidelines. We searched four major electronic databases from inception to April 2026. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies enrolling adult patients with respiratory failure secondary to AHF or acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, comparing HFNC and NIV. The primary outcome was composite treatment failure. Secondary outcomes included endotracheal intubation, short-term mortality, arterial blood gas (ABG) parameters, respiratory rate, dyspnea scores, and hospital length of stay. A random-effects model was used. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Ten studies (n = 1,282 patients) were included, comprising five RCTs and five observational studies. HFNC showed no statistically significant difference compared with NIV in the composite outcome of treatment failure (RR = 1.22, 95% CI: 0.81-1.84), endotracheal intubation (RR = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.58-1.28), or short-term mortality (RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.69-1.42). Design-stratified estimates for treatment failure also crossed the line of no effect in both RCTs (RR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.61-1.63) and observational studies (RR = 1.44, 95% CI: 0.77-2.69). No statistically significant differences were observed in ABG parameters, respiratory rate, dyspnea scores, or hospital length of stay. The GRADE assessment showed predominantly moderate certainty evidence for RCT comparisons, with high-certainty evidence for changes in PaCO2 and pH. The available evidence did not find a statistically significant difference between HFNC and NIV in terms of clinical efficacy in patients with AHF-related respiratory failure. HFNC may be considered in selected patients who do not tolerate NIV, provided that close monitoring and prompt access to NIV escalation are available. Although the certainty of evidence was generally moderate for RCTs comparisons, further adequately powered multicenter RCTs are needed to better define patient selection and clinically important differences. www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261330512, identifier CRD420261330512.

title: Precipitants of Acute Heart Failure: A State-of-the-art Review from an International Expert Group.
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is a leading cause of hospitalisation worldwide, with the majority of cases triggered by an identifiable precipitant. Recognition of these precipitants is important for both acute management and long-term prevention, as they are frequently reversible, carry prognostic significance and directly inform targeted therapy. The epidemiology of precipitants varies across settings, and patterns are evolving as the prevalence of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction rises. In this review, we summarise the epidemiology, diagnostic evaluation and management of the most common precipitants of AHF. Globally, the leading precipitants of AHF are ischaemia/acute coronary syndrome, infection, arrhythmias, uncontrolled hypertension, nonadherence and renal dysfunction, although their relative distribution varies by geography and heart failure phenotype. Optimal medical management necessitates initial haemodynamic stabilisation, identification of the underlying precipitant and delivery of targeted therapy. Importantly, successful identification and treatment of a reversible precipitant should not preclude initiation or optimisation of guideline-directed medical therapy, which remain essential for long-term outcomes.

title: High-Flow Nasal Oxygen Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy and Non-Invasive Ventilation for Acute Respiratory Failure in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compares the use of high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) with conventional oxygen therapy (COT) and non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in the management of acute respiratory failure (ARF) in the emergency department (ED). A comprehensive search of relevant sources was undertaken. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing adult patients (≥ 18 years) treated in the ED for ARF and comparing HFNO to COT/NIV were included. The primary outcome was the need for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation (IMV). Secondary outcomes included physiological and biochemical parameters, ICU admission, hospital length of stay, dyspnoea scores and mortality. A total of 17 RCTs (1955 patients) were included. There was a significant reduction in IMV favouring the HFNO group compared to COT and NIV (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.47-0.88). HFNO showed significant improvements in RR, SpO2, PaO2 and Modified Borg Dyspnoea Scale. Subgroup analysis showed reduced rates of IMV with HFNO compared to COT (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41-0.91), but not compared to NIV (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.42-1.14). HFNO additionally showed a reduction of IMV compared to NIV and COT in undifferentiated patients (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41-0.93), but not in exacerbations of COPD or acute heart failure. Ten of the 17 studies had at least some concern for risk of bias, with several analyses having notable heterogeneity. HFNO showed a significant reduction in rates of IMV, improvement in peripheral oxygen saturations, PaO2, respiratory rate and patient dyspnoea scores compared to COT and NIV.

title: Liver Function Abnormalities in Acute Heart Failure: A State-of-the-art Review from an International Expert Group.
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is a systemic condition characterised by multiorgan involvement that varies from subclinical to overt organ failure. The liver is particularly vulnerable due to its dual blood supply and sensitivity to haemodynamic and inflammatory disturbances. Abnormal liver function tests are highly prevalent in patients with AHF, reflecting major mechanisms: passive hepatic venous congestion from elevated central venous pressure, hepatocellular ischaemia from low cardiac output, systemic inflammation and poor metabolic status associated with cachexia. In patients with AHF, liver function tests at admission, during hospitalisation and at discharge are independently associated with rehospitalisation, cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Persistent abnormalities after hospitalisation often reflect incomplete decongestion or irreversible structural liver changes. Therapeutic strategies focus on decongestion, optimisation of cardiac output and medication adjustments to avoid hepatotoxicity. Despite significant advances in understanding cardio-hepatic interactions, major gaps remain, including the lack of standardised definitions, limited mechanistic studies and the underrepresentation of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in contemporary research. Future research should explore targeted therapies to improve cardiohepatic interactions and patient outcomes.
